explain.say: In 1543 a Polish church official, Nicolaus Copernicus, published a book putting the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the planets. Less than 150 years later Isaac Newton explained the motion of planets and falling apples with the same laws. Historians call this the Scientific Revolution. Look at the timeline.

explain.say: Look at the middle dots. Kepler showed planets move in ellipses, Galileo's telescope revealed moons around Jupiter, and Harvey showed blood circulates. Bacon urged knowledge built from experiment. In 1633 the Church forced Galileo to recant. Why might a new idea about the sky feel threatening?

explain.say: Copernicus did not work alone. See the network. Astronomers at Maragha in Iran, like Nasir al-Din al-Tusi in the 1200s, built mathematical models that appear in Copernicus's book, though how he learned of them is debated. Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand mapped the stars in the 1420s. Which link surprises you?

Look at the map, from Iran and Samarkand to Poland, Italy and England. In India, the Kerala school of mathematicians, from Madhava around 1400, found infinite series for pi centuries before Europeans did similar work, though no influence on Europe is proven. Why might ideas travel, or not?

See the debate. Herbert Butterfield, in 1949, called it the biggest change since Christianity began; Steven Shapin argued there was no single revolution, just many messy changes. Fantastic work. Exam tip: name one non-European contribution and one continuity with older ideas.

faq.a: The changes in Europe from about 1543, with Copernicus, to 1687, with Newton's Principia, when new ideas in astronomy, physics, anatomy and method, based on mathematics and experiment, replaced much of Aristotle's natural philosophy.
In Principia, 1687, Isaac Newton set out three laws of motion and universal gravitation, showing that the same mathematical laws govern falling objects on Earth and the orbits of planets.

faq.q: Why was Galileo put on trial?
faq.a: In 1633 the Roman Inquisition tried Galileo for defending Copernicus's Sun-centred system, which Church authorities had condemned in 1616. He was made to recant and kept under house arrest until his death in 1642.

Copernicus used mathematical devices, such as the Tusi couple, first developed by astronomers at the Maragha observatory in Iran. Historians like George Saliba argue for transmission, though the exact route to Copernicus is still debated.

A group of mathematicians and astronomers in Kerala, India, from Madhava of Sangamagrama around 1400, who found infinite series for pi and trigonometric functions centuries before similar results in Europe. Any influence on Europe is unproven.
